title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment (N = 300 matched intents) to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations in an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen adapter contract we generated one shared LLM candidate per paired intent (model_calls_used = 300) and evaluated two deterministic validators combined by a logical-OR decision rule. Confirmatory outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (paired contingency n11 = 300; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). McNemar two-sided p = 1.0; bootstrap 95% CI for the paired risk-difference = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Critically, because no validator ever flagged a forbidden reachability, the repair path was never invoked and the preregistered hypothesis about repair efficacy is untestable in this run. The paper therefore (a) reports deterministic execution and archival artifacts that support reproducibility, (b) quantifies the degenerate statistical outcome and its operational implications, and (c) draws artifact-grounded design lessons for follow-up stress tests intended to exercise the repair path (independent-generation semantics, stronger adversaries, higher repair budgets, and richer verifiers).

sections.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) can generate network-device configurations from natural-language operator intents, but incorrect or unchecked outputs risk expanding an operator's attack surface by enabling forbidden connectivity or violating policy. Prior system and survey research therefore recommends constrained generation, execution oracles, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) architectures as operational mitigations. However, preregistered, execution‑accountable evidence that a verifier-in-the-loop meaningfully reduces security-increasing misconfigurations under adversarial intents is limited.

We designed and preregistered a paired confirmatory study to answer a focused operational question: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier in a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden‑reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? The run was executed under a frozen protocol (study cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1) and deterministic orchestration. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered, deterministic paired execution with archived per-episode validator traces and provider-call accounting; (2) a concise, artifact-grounded report of a degenerate confirmatory outcome (no validator-detected violations in either arm) and its statistical interpretation; (3) a compact technical definition of the security predicate and a brief summary of the validators used; and (4) artifact-grounded design recommendations for follow-up stress tests that can exercise the repair path.
sections.related_work: Research on LLM-augmented NetOps has converged on two relevant themes. First, generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures often improve correctness for code and infrastructure artifacts when verifiers provide meaningful failure signals; such system work highlights that verifier power and repair strategy determine realized gains (e.g., verifier-feedback IaC work). Second, surveys and NetOps system papers document LLM failure modes—hallucination, domain mismatch, and overconfidence—and recommend integrating validators, constrained generation, or human oversight to reduce operational risk. Third, emulation/testbed research confirms that execution-based validation is feasible in controlled settings but warns of external-validity gaps to production devices and live traffic. Our study is positioned as a narrowly scoped, preregistered, execution-accountable test that complements these lines by reporting deterministic artifacts and a concrete degenerate outcome that informs experimental design choices.
sections.methodology:
Design and preregistration: The preregistered confirmatory design fixed a paired binary estimand (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline) on N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants). The primary test was a paired McNemar exact test (alpha = 0.05); prespecified CIs were to be computed by bootstrap percentile methods. Sampling, deduplication, contamination flags, exclusion rules, and sensitivity analyses were frozen in the preregistration.

Generation semantics and adapter contract: To limit model-call cost we executed under a shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each intent pair we generated a single LLM candidate and replayed that candidate to both arms (baseline = direct replay; guarded = validator checked and allowed up to one repair LLM call if a validator reported forbidden reachability). This contract reduced hosted-model generations to one per pair (model_calls_used = 300 for 300 pairs) and is recorded in the execution manifest.

Operational definition of the security predicate and validators (concise): The forbidden‑reachability predicate operationalizes whether the generated configuration produces any new, undesired reachability relative to the task-specified constraints (tasks contain explicit protected interfaces such as mgmt1 and workflow policies that forbid certain new connectivity patterns). We implemented two deterministic validators: (1) a Batfish-style execution validator that runs the candidate configuration in the Dockerized FRRouting-style emulator and inspects control‑plane and forwarding reachability for predicate violations; and (2) a lightweight Python graph-based static reachability analyzer that computes reachability over a device‑graph abstraction. The two validators were combined with a logical-OR decision rule: any validator reporting a forbidden-reachability predicate marks the episode as violating and would trigger the preregistered repair attempt. Full per-episode validator traces and task payload constraints (including protected_interfaces and workflow_policies) are archived in the evidence bundle for audit.

Intervention and repair policy: Baseline arm = replayed shared candidate; Guarded arm = same candidate validated and, if violating, sent one repair prompt to the LLM (max one repair per pair, as preregistered). Repair was only to be invoked upon a validator-detected forbidden reachability.

Execution and determinism: The environment used deterministic Docker compositions (FRRouting-style images) and seeded task generation. Provider-call accounting, seeds, raw responses, validator traces, and scoring artifacts were archived to permit deterministic replay.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed all planned episodes (completed_episode_count = 600; 300 pairs across two conditions) with zero failed episodes and model_calls_used = 300 under the shared_initial_candidate contract. Provider-call auditing shows stage_counts = {'shared_initial_generation': 300}.

Primary confirmatory outcome: Every paired intent passed the forbidden‑reachability predicate in both arms. Contingency counts (paired table): n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (Table 1). Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided test: p = 1.0. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired risk-difference (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Observing 0/300 violations implies a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on the baseline violation probability ≈ 0.00994.

Repair activity and verifier concordance: Because no validator reported forbidden reachability on any shared initial candidate, no repair calls were invoked and all per-episode repair_applied flags are false. Validator judgments were concordant for every episode (verifier_disagreement_rate = 0 in archived artifacts).

Representative examples and artifact pointers: Representative shared-initial responses and scoring traces (e.g., task-000001) show normalized configurations, validator validation_before/after entries, and the repair_applied = false flags. The key artifacts supporting these numeric outcomes are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/scoring/*.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv).
sections.discussion:
Statistical and inferential meaning: The observed contingency is degenerate — no discordant pairs exist — and therefore the paired McNemar test is uninformative for the preregistered confirmatory question about repair efficacy. Two coupled, artifact-documented design facts produced this degeneracy: (1) the shared_initial_candidate contract reuses a single LLM candidate per pair and thereby reduces between-arm sampling variance that could produce discordant failures; and (2) for the chosen model, validators, and adversarial perturbations the initial candidates were validator‑compliant for all sampled intents. Thus the run substantiates a narrow descriptive claim: under the executed contract and testbed the verifier-insertion did not change observed compliance because baseline was already compliant; it does not support a claim that verifiers cannot rescue violations in other settings.

Operational lessons (artifact-grounded): (a) Generation semantics matter — for experiments intended to exercise repair efficacy, independent-condition generation (two independent LLM draws per pair) or larger repair-call budgets increase the probability of observing discordant violating outputs at the expense of provider cost (the execution manifest records maximum_model_calls = 600). (b) Adversary potency matters — programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability for the tested model and validators; stronger or targeted adversaries are needed to exercise repair paths. (c) Verifier strength and diversity matter — a single verifier family may under-detect some classes of violations; combining diverse oracles and including production-grade oracles improves construct validity. (d) Reproducibility is practical — per-episode raw responses, validator traces, and provider-call audits were archived and permit deterministic reanalysis and targeted stress tests.

Threats to validity (concise artifact references): Internal validity is limited by shared_initial_candidate semantics and single‑model scope (execution/model_configuration.json, deterministic_reconciliation.json). Construct validity depends on whether the forbidden‑reachability predicate (task workflow_policies and protected_interfaces) and the two deterministic validators adequately represent operational security requirements; validators and their limitations are recorded in execution/scoring/*.json. External validity is limited because tasks were synthetic and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Conclusion validity is constrained because the preregistered power assumption (nonzero baseline violation rate) was not met and the primary hypothesis was therefore untestable. We enumerate these threats and point to the archived artifacts for replication and more targeted follow-up tests.
sections.conclusion: We report a preregistered, deterministically executed paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation. The run completed N = 300 matched pairs with model_calls_used = 300 under a shared_initial_candidate contract and produced a degenerate confirmatory outcome: both baseline and guarded arms passed the forbidden‑reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never signaled violations, the repair path was never exercised and the primary preregistered hypothesis about repair efficacy is untestable in this execution. The main scientific value of the study is therefore empirical: (1) precise, archived execution accounting that quantifies the cost–variance trade-offs of shared vs independent generation semantics; (2) a tight descriptive bound on undetected baseline violations (one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994); and (3) artifact-grounded design recommendations for follow-up stress tests designed to exercise the repair mechanism and to assess verifier rescue capability under stronger adversaries, independent draws, multi-model comparisons, and richer oracles. We release the preregistration, per-episode validator traces, provider-call audit, and analysis artifacts to enable deterministic reanalysis and targeted future experiments that can address the untested repair question explicitly by altering generation semantics, adversary strength, and repair budgets.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render the paired McNemar test uninformative about repair efficacy when baseline violation rates are nonzero; the preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted detecting a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction.

GVR not exercised: under the chosen task set, emulator, model, and validators the verifier never reported forbidden reachability and consequently the guarded repair step was never invoked; the experiment therefore tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced one LLM call per pair and reduced model-call overhead but also limited independent draws that could produce discordant errors; alternative contracts (independent-condition generation or expanded repair budgets) would better exercise repair paths.

Adversarial-perturbation detail: the preregistration specified programmatic generation of one adversarial variant per benign seed; per-task generation seeds and intent payloads are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl and transformation logs in the execution manifest for reproducibility.

External validity: tasks were synthetically generated and executed in Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation; results do not necessarily generalize to heterogeneous production devices, live traffic, or different operational constraints.
Model and verifier scope: a single model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; other LLMs, stronger verifiers, or dynamic execution oracles may produce different outcomes.
